decks.title: Directing — Part 1: Meaning, Importance, Supervision and Motivation
goals: Explain why directing is needed to turn plans into action
Describe the functions of a supervisor and explain span of control
Explain Maslow's hierarchy of needs and suggest incentives suited to each level

slides.heading: Directing
slides.body_md: Part 1: what **directing** is, why it **matters**, **supervision** and **span of control**, and **motivation** through Maslow's needs.

visual.alt: Route map of Part 1: the meaning and importance of directing, supervision and span of control, and motivation with Maslow's need hierarchy
visual.caption: Part 1 at a glance

slides.narration: A firm may have excellent plans, a neat structure and the right people, yet nothing happens until someone tells people what to do, shows them how, and makes them want to do it well. That is directing. In this part we look at its meaning and importance, at supervision, and at motivation.

slides.heading: What is directing?
slides.body_md: **Directing** means **instructing, guiding, supervising, motivating and leading** people so that they work towards the goals of the organisation.

rows: Watches and guides work on the floor
Makes people want to give their best
Passes ideas and instructions both ways

visual.alt: Table of the four elements of directing (supervision, motivation, leadership and communication) with what the manager does in each

slides.narration: Directing is the function that puts people into action. It has four elements. Supervision is watching and guiding work. Motivation makes people want to give their best. Leadership influences them to follow willingly. Communication carries ideas and instructions up and down the organisation.

slides.heading: Features of directing

rows: Work starts only when people are told and guided
Done at every level and in every kind of organisation
Goes on throughout the life of the organisation
Each superior directs the people just below

visual.alt: Table of four features of directing: it initiates action, is pervasive, is continuous and flows from top to bottom

slides.narration: Directing has four features. It initiates action, because work begins only when people are guided. It is pervasive, found at every level and in every kind of organisation. It is continuous, going on every working day. And it flows downwards, each superior directing the people just below.

slides.heading: Why directing matters

rows: Makes each person's work fit the whole

visual.alt: Table of five points of importance of directing with a short meaning for each

slides.narration: Directing matters in five ways. It turns plans into action. It integrates the efforts of many people so that their work fits together. It motivates people to give their best. It keeps teams in balance. And it helps a firm bring in change, because people who are guided and reassured resist less.

slides.heading: Quick check: continuous or one-time?
slides.body_md: True or false: directing is carried out once, when a new plan is introduced.
slides.narration: Think about what managers do every working day.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: which importance?
slides.body_md: Match each imagined situation with the point of importance of directing it shows.
bullets: Step 1: find the **clue** in the situation.
Step 2: name the point of importance.
Step 3: explain it in one line.

rows: Dyers, weavers and packers time their work to fit one another
Clerks are trained and reassured before tablets replace registers
New bakers start work once recipes are explained
Praise and fair rewards lift a team's output

visual.alt: Worked table matching four imagined workplace situations with the point of importance of directing each shows
visual.caption: Look for the clue: fitting work together, a change, starting work, or effort.

slides.narration: Let us practise. Teams timing their work to fit one another shows integration of efforts. Training and reassuring clerks before a new system shows that directing eases change. Bakers starting once recipes are explained shows that directing initiates action. Praise lifting output shows directing as a means of motivation.

slides.heading: Supervision
slides.body_md: **Supervision** is overseeing subordinates at work and guiding them so that work is done as planned. The **supervisor** is the first-line manager.

rows: Explains new targets; reports workers' problems
Decides who runs which machine today
Ensures work is done as planned
Checks quality and output every hour
Shows a new welder how to hold the torch
Settles a quarrel; praises a good team

visual.alt: Table of five functions of a supervisor with a shop-floor example of each

slides.narration: The supervisor works closest to the workers. She links management and workers, plans and assigns daily work, checks that it is done as planned, trains new joiners on the job, and keeps the group united and in good spirits.

slides.body_md: **Span of control** is the number of subordinates one superior can supervise **effectively**.

slides.narration: How many people can one supervisor guide well? That number is the span of control. A narrow span means few subordinates and close guidance, but more supervisors are needed. A wide span means many subordinates and lower cost, but less attention for each person.

slides.heading: What decides the span?

visual.alt: Table of four factors that decide the span of control, showing when each calls for a narrow span and when it allows a wide span

slides.narration: Four factors decide the span. Complex work needs a narrow span, while simple, repeated work allows a wide one. A skilled supervisor can handle more people. Trained workers need less help. And quick, easy ways of communicating let one supervisor look after more people.

slides.narration: Abraham Maslow said people have five kinds of needs, arranged like a ladder. First come physiological needs such as food and shelter. Then safety, then social needs for belonging, then esteem, and at the top self-actualisation, becoming all one can be. People move up as lower needs are reasonably met, and a satisfied need no longer motivates.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: matching incentives to needs
slides.body_md: Four imagined employees, each with a different active need.
bullets: Step 1: see which needs are **already met**.
Step 2: the next level up is the **active need**.
Step 3: choose an incentive for that level.

rows: New helper who cannot pay rent
Senior engineer with everything else met

visual.alt: Worked table: four imagined employees, the need that is active for each and a matching incentive
visual.caption: First find which needs are already met; the next one up is active.

slides.narration: A helper who cannot pay rent has an active physiological need, so a wage on time helps most. Crews without contracts seek safety. A recruit far from home seeks belonging. A senior engineer whose other needs are met seeks self-actualisation, so a challenging project of his own will motivate him best.

slides.heading: Quick check: which need?
slides.body_md: A new helper wants above all a wage that covers food and rent. Which need is this?
slides.narration: Start at the bottom of the ladder.

slides.heading: Summary of Part 1

rows: Instructing, guiding, supervising, motivating and leading people
Initiates action, integrates, motivates, stabilises, eases change

visual.alt: Summary table of Part 1: directing, its importance, supervision and span of control, and Maslow's needs

slides.narration: To sum up Part 1. Directing instructs, guides, supervises, motivates and leads people. It initiates action, integrates efforts, motivates, brings balance and eases change. The supervisor guides workers directly, and the span of control sets how many each can handle. Maslow ranks needs from physiological to self-actualisation.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: Name all four **elements** of directing when asked for its meaning.
For span of control, link the size to the **nature of work**.
Learn Maslow's needs **in order**, bottom to top.
Match each incentive to the **next unmet need**, not one already met.

visual.alt: Three steps for case questions: quote the clue from the case, name the concept, and explain it or suggest a remedy

slides.narration: Some tips. When defining directing, mention its four elements. When asked about span of control, connect it to the nature of work and the skill of people. Learn Maslow's five needs in order. In case questions, find which needs are already met, and suggest an incentive for the next one.

decks.title: Directing — Part 2: Leadership and Communication
goals: Identify the leadership style used in a given situation
Draw and explain the communication process
Identify barriers to communication in a case and suggest ways to overcome them

slides.heading: Leadership and Communication
slides.body_md: Part 2: **leadership** and its four **styles**, the **communication process**, and **barriers** to communication with their remedies.

visual.alt: Route map of Part 2: leadership and its four styles, the communication process, and barriers to communication with ways to overcome them
visual.caption: Part 2 at a glance

slides.narration: In Part 2 we look at two more elements of directing. First, leadership, and the four styles a leader may use. Then communication, how a message travels from sender to receiver, what can block it, and how managers can clear the way.

slides.heading: What is leadership?
slides.body_md: **Leadership** is the ability to **influence** the behaviour of people so that they work **willingly** towards group goals.

visual.alt: Flow showing leadership: the leader influences followers, who give willing effort towards group goals
visual.caption: Leadership is influence, not just authority.

slides.narration: A manager has authority because of her post, but a leader gets people to follow willingly. Leadership is the ability to influence people so that they put in willing effort towards shared goals. Good managers try to be good leaders too.

slides.heading: Four styles of leadership

rows: Members are left free to act

visual.alt: Table of four leadership styles showing who decides under each and a one-line meaning

slides.narration: We need only the meaning of four styles. An autocratic leader decides alone and expects obedience. A democratic leader invites ideas and decides with the group. A laissez-faire leader leaves the group free to decide and act. A bureaucratic leader goes strictly by rules and procedures.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: name the style
bullets: Step 1: ask **who decides**.
Step 2: ask **on what basis**: personal will, discussion, freedom or rules.
Step 3: name the style.

rows: Yard manager gives exact orders before a deadline; no discussion
Plant head invites suggestions on shift timings and decides with workers
Editor leaves expert writers free to plan their own stories
Depot manager decides leave strictly by the rule book

visual.alt: Worked table matching four imagined situations with the leadership style each shows
visual.caption: Ask: who takes the decision, and on what basis?

slides.narration: A yard manager giving exact orders with no discussion is autocratic. A plant head who invites suggestions and decides with workers is democratic. An editor who leaves expert writers free is laissez-faire. A depot manager who decides leave strictly by the rule book is bureaucratic, because rules, not his own will, decide.

slides.heading: Quick check: rules decide
slides.body_md: A depot manager decides every leave request strictly by the rule book. Which style?
slides.narration: Ask whether the leader or the rules make the decision.

slides.heading: Communication and its objectives
slides.body_md: **Communication** is the exchange of ideas, facts and feelings between people to create **common understanding**.

rows: Praise for a team that met its target
Linking the work of two sections
A talk on a new machine
Workers raise problems in a meeting

visual.alt: Table of five objectives of communication in an organisation with an example of each

slides.narration: Communication runs through every part of directing. In a firm it serves several objectives: to inform and instruct, to motivate, to coordinate the work of different sections, to educate and train, and to get feedback and build good relations.

slides.heading: The communication process
bullets: **Sender** has an idea and **encodes** it.
The **message** travels through a **channel**.
The **receiver** **decodes** it.
**Feedback** goes back to the sender; **noise** can disturb any stage.

visual.alt: Communication process: the sender encodes an idea into a message, which travels through a channel; the receiver decodes it, and feedback returns from the receiver to the sender
visual.caption: Feedback returns from receiver to sender; noise can disturb any stage.

slides.narration: The sender has an idea and encodes it into words or symbols. The message travels through a channel such as a notice, call or meeting. The receiver decodes it to find the meaning. Feedback then goes back to the sender. Noise, anything that disturbs the message, can creep in at any stage.

slides.heading: Quick check: an analogy
slides.body_md: Complete the analogy. Sender : Encoding :: Receiver : ___
slides.narration: What does the receiver do to a message?

slides.heading: Barriers to communication

visual.alt: Table of four kinds of barriers to communication, where each arises from and an example of each

slides.narration: Messages fail for four kinds of reasons. Semantic barriers come from words, such as jargon or poor translation. Psychological barriers come from feelings such as distrust or fear. Organisational barriers come from rules and too many levels. Personal barriers come from the attitudes of superiors or subordinates.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: barriers and remedies
slides.body_md: Four problems at an imagined workshop.
bullets: Step 1: find the **cause** of the problem.
Step 2: name the **barrier**.
Step 3: suggest a **remedy** that removes that cause.

rows: Notice uses words workers do not know
Workers fear change means job cuts
Head looks annoyed when asked questions

visual.alt: Worked table: four problems at an imagined workshop, the barrier behind each and a remedy
visual.caption: Name the barrier first, then give a remedy that fits it.

slides.narration: Words the workers do not know are a semantic barrier, so use simple local words. Fear of job cuts is psychological, so meet workers honestly. Ideas passing through four officers is organisational, so cut layers. A head who looks annoyed at questions shows a personal barrier, so he must learn to listen.

slides.heading: Overcoming barriers

rows: The sender knows exactly what to say
Ask for feedback and follow up

visual.alt: Table of five ways to overcome barriers to communication and why each helps

slides.narration: Managers can clear the way in several ways. Clarify the idea before speaking. Use words the receiver knows. Consult people and listen to them. Ask for feedback and follow up. Above all, make actions match words, because that is what slowly removes distrust.

slides.heading: Quick check: rigid forms
slides.body_md: Suggestions must pass three signatures on a set form, so workers stop making them. Which barrier?
slides.narration: Is the problem in words, feelings, rules, or a person?

slides.heading: Summary of Part 2

rows: Influencing people to work willingly towards goals
Sender, encoding, channel, decoding, receiver, feedback; noise
Semantic, psychological, organisational, personal; each has remedies

visual.alt: Summary table of Part 2: leadership, the four styles, the communication process and barriers

slides.narration: To sum up Part 2. Leadership is influencing people to work willingly. The four styles are autocratic, democratic, laissez-faire and bureaucratic. Communication moves from sender through encoding, channel and decoding to the receiver, with feedback returning. Barriers may be semantic, psychological, organisational or personal, and each can be overcome.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: For styles, ask **who decides** and **on what basis**.
Draw the process as **sender → encoding → channel → decoding → receiver**, with **feedback** back.
Name the **type** of barrier before giving a remedy.
Make each remedy **fit the cause** in the case.

visual.alt: Three steps for case questions: quote the clue from the case, name the concept, and explain it or suggest a remedy

slides.narration: Final tips. To spot a style, ask who decides and on what basis. When drawing the process, show feedback returning to the sender. In barrier questions, name the type first, then give a remedy that removes that very cause. Quote the clue from the case each time.

sections.heading: 1. Meaning, features and importance of directing
sections.body_md:
**Directing** is the function of management that **instructs, guides, supervises, motivates and leads** people so that they work towards organisational goals. Its four **elements** are supervision, motivation, leadership and communication.

**Features:** it **initiates action**; it is **pervasive** (every level, every organisation); it is **continuous**; it **flows from top to bottom**.

**Importance:**
- **Initiates action** — plans become work only when people are guided.
- **Integrates efforts** — each person's work is linked to the work of others.
- **Means of motivation** — guidance and rewards bring out people's potential.
- **Stability and balance** — leadership and communication keep teams in step.
- **Facilitates change** — explaining and reassuring reduces resistance to new methods.

sections.heading: 2. Supervision and span of control
sections.body_md:
**Supervision** means overseeing people at work and guiding them so that work is done according to plan. The **supervisor** is the first-line manager in direct daily contact with workers.

**Functions of a supervisor:** link between management and workers; planning and assigning daily work; ensuring work meets targets and standards; on-the-job training; maintaining group unity; building morale; giving feedback upward and downward.

**Span of control** is the number of subordinates one superior can supervise effectively. A **narrow span** gives closer guidance but needs more supervisors; a **wide span** costs less but gives less attention to each worker.

**Factors:** nature of work; ability of the supervisor; competence of workers; communication methods; how spread out the workers are.

sections.heading: 3. Motivation and Maslow's need hierarchy
sections.body_md:
**Motivation** is the process of stimulating people to act willingly towards desired goals by satisfying their needs. A **motive** is an inner urge; a **motivator** (incentive) is what a manager offers to satisfy it.

**Maslow's hierarchy** (bottom to top):
1. **Physiological** — food, clothing, shelter; met by basic pay.
2. **Safety** — security of job and income; met by permanent posts, pension, insurance.
3. **Social** — belonging and friendship; met by teamwork and friendly groups.
4. **Esteem** — status, recognition, self-respect; met by titles, awards, praise.
5. **Self-actualisation** — becoming what one is capable of; met by challenging work and autonomy.

**Assumptions:** behaviour depends on needs; needs are in an order; a person moves up when a lower need is reasonably met; a satisfied need no longer motivates.

sections.heading: 4. Leadership and its styles
sections.body_md:
**Leadership** is the ability of a person to influence others so that they work willingly and enthusiastically towards group goals.

**Styles (meaning only):**
- **Autocratic** — the leader keeps decision-making power and expects obedience.
- **Democratic (participative)** — the leader consults the group and decides with them.
- **Laissez-faire (free-rein)** — the group is left largely free to decide and act; the leader supports when asked.
- **Bureaucratic** — the leader manages strictly by rules, procedures and official channels.

sections.heading: 5. Communication: objectives, process, barriers
sections.body_md:
**Communication** is the exchange of facts, ideas and feelings between people so as to create common understanding.

**Objectives:** to inform and instruct; motivate; coordinate; educate and train; obtain feedback; build good relations.

**Process:** sender → **encoding** → message → **channel** → **decoding** → receiver → **feedback** to the sender. **Noise** is any disturbance that distorts the message at any stage.

**Barriers:**
- **Semantic** — jargon, words with several meanings, faulty translation.
- **Psychological** — distrust, fear, premature evaluation, poor attention.
- **Organisational** — rigid rules, too many levels, lack of facilities.
- **Personal** — superiors who will not listen or subordinates who hesitate to speak.

**Overcoming them:** clarify the idea first; use the receiver's language; consult and listen; seek feedback and follow up; keep actions consistent with words.

questions.stem_md: At Lushai Handlooms, an imagined weaving unit in Aizawl, the plan for the winter shawl collection is ready and twenty weavers have been hired. Which function of management will now set the work moving by instructing, guiding and encouraging the weavers?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Directing. Plans and people are in place; instructing, guiding, supervising and motivating them so that work actually starts is directing.

It brings stability by controlling costs
It replaces the need for planning
It integrates the efforts of employees

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** It integrates the efforts of employees. By guiding each team and linking their work, the manager makes individual efforts fit together; directing integrates employees' efforts.

questions.stem_md: When Kallai Timber Mart, an imagined timber yard in Kozhikode, replaced paper registers with tablets, the manager explained the benefits to the clerks, listened to their fears and arranged training, so the new system was accepted without protest. This shows that directing

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Directing is said to initiate action in an organisation.

**Reason (R):** Directing is performed by managers at every level, from the chief executive to the supervisor.

Choose the correct option.

Both Assertion and Reason are true but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are false.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Both statements are true. Directing initiates action because work starts only when people are instructed and guided; the fact that every level performs it (pervasiveness) is true but does not explain this.

questions.solution_md: **False.** False. Managers instruct, guide and motivate people every working day, so directing goes on throughout the life of the organisation.

questions.solution_md: Any two points of importance (initiates action, integrates efforts, motivates, brings stability, facilitates change), linked to the new plant.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **It initiates action:** new staff start work only when managers **instruct and guide** them on recipes and machines.
2. **It integrates efforts:** guidance links the mixing, baking and packing teams so their work **fits together** towards the plant's targets.

1. **Pervasive:** directing is done at **every level**, from the chief executive to the duty manager.
2. **Continuous:** it goes on **every shift, year after year**, not once.
3. **Flows from top to bottom:** each superior directs the people **just below**, so instructions move **downward** through the airline.

(a) What is meant by directing? [1]
(b) Shivnath Steel Fabricators, an imagined firm in Bhilai, is installing robotic welding cells and many welders fear for their jobs. Explain four ways in which directing will help the firm through this change. [4]
questions.solution_md: Meaning; four points of importance applied to the change at the firm.

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) **Directing** is the management function of **instructing, guiding, supervising, motivating and leading** people so that they work towards the organisation's goals.

(b) 1. **Facilitates change:** managers **explain** why robots are coming and how welders' jobs will change, which reduces fear and resistance.

questions.stem_md: Arvind, a senior engineer at Waltair Marine Fittings, an imagined firm in Visakhapatnam, has a good salary, a secure job, close friends at work and a respected title. He now wants to design a new propeller entirely by himself to see how far his abilities can take him. Which need is now active?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Self-actualisation need. His lower needs are met; the urge to realise his full potential is self-actualisation, the highest need.

questions.stem_md: Workers at Subarnarekha Agro Tools, an imagined maker of farm tools in Ranchi, earn fair wages, have permanent jobs and get on well with one another. According to Maslow, which incentive is most likely to motivate them further?

options.text_md: A small rise in the canteen subsidy
Public recognition of good work and promotion to a respected title

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Public recognition of good work and promotion to a respected title. Physiological, safety and social needs are satisfied, so they no longer motivate much; esteem needs are next, and recognition and status meet them.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** A need that is reasonably satisfied no longer motivates a person strongly.

**Reason (R):** According to Maslow, once a lower need is reasonably met, the next higher need becomes the main motivator.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are false.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Both are true, and the reason explains the assertion: behaviour is driven by the next unmet need, not by needs already met.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** According to Maslow, self-actualisation is the first need that a new worker tries to satisfy.

**Reason (R):** Physiological needs are at the top of Maslow's need hierarchy.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are false.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Both statements are false. Physiological needs come first and sit at the bottom of the hierarchy; self-actualisation is at the top and comes last.

questions.stem_md: In Maslow's hierarchy, esteem needs come below safety needs.
questions.solution_md: **False.** False. The order from the bottom is physiological, safety, social, esteem and self-actualisation, so esteem is above safety.

questions.stem_md: In Maslow's hierarchy, the need for status, recognition and self-respect is called the ___ need.
questions.solution_md: These form the esteem (ego) need.

questions.stem_md: Match each incentive offered at Dharwad Pedha House, an imagined sweet maker in Hubballi, with the need it mainly satisfies.

options.text_md: A fair basic wage paid on time
Provident fund and a written job contract
The title "Master Confectioner" for a senior cook

questions.solution_md: **Key:** (a)–(r), (b)–(p), (c)–(s), (d)–(q). Wages meet basic needs; provident fund and contracts give security; shared celebrations meet the need to belong; a respected title meets esteem.

questions.stem_md: State two assumptions on which Maslow's need hierarchy theory rests.
questions.solution_md: Any two assumptions (needs drive behaviour; hierarchical order; satisfied need stops motivating; move up once a lower need is met).

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Behaviour depends on needs:** people act in order to **satisfy unmet needs**.
2. **Needs follow an order:** a person moves to a **higher need** only after the **lower one is reasonably satisfied**, and a satisfied need no longer motivates.

questions.stem_md: Suggest one suitable incentive for each employee of Chilika Seafoods (imagined), Puri: (i) Sunita, a new packer who struggles to pay her rent; (ii) Gopal, a senior quality checker who wants respect for his twenty years of service.
questions.solution_md: An incentive matched to each person's active need.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) Sunita has an unmet **physiological need**: a **fair wage paid on time** or a small **advance** would motivate her.
(ii) Gopal seeks **esteem**: **public recognition**, a long-service award or a senior title would motivate him.

questions.stem_md: Tawi Dry Fruits (imagined), Jammu, pays fair wages and offers secure jobs, yet workers say that nobody notices their effort and they rarely meet as a team. Using Maslow's theory, identify two unmet needs with an incentive for each, and name the need the firm should plan for next.
questions.solution_md: Social and esteem needs identified with incentives; self-actualisation named as the next level.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Social need:** workers rarely meet as a team; **team outings, shared lunch breaks** or group projects would meet it.
2. **Esteem need:** effort goes unnoticed; **recognition schemes, praise** and titles for good work would meet it.
3. **Next: self-actualisation.** Once these are met, the firm should offer **challenging tasks, autonomy** and chances to learn.

questions.stem_md:
(a) Define motivation. [1]
(b) The HR manager of Kallai Timber Mart (imagined), Kozhikode, wants a ladder of incentives for her staff. Using Maslow's theory, name the five needs from the lowest to the highest and suggest one incentive for each. [4]
questions.solution_md: Definition; five needs in order, each with a suitable incentive.

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) **Motivation** is the process of **stimulating people to act willingly** towards desired goals by **satisfying their needs**.

(b) 1. **Physiological needs:** food, clothing, shelter — a **fair wage paid on time** and meal allowances.
2. **Safety needs:** security of job and income — **permanent posts, provident fund** and insurance.
3. **Social needs:** belonging and friendship — **team events** and friendly work groups.
4. **Esteem needs:** status and recognition — **awards, titles and praise** in staff meetings.
5. **Self-actualisation needs:** realising one's potential — **challenging projects**, freedom to try new methods and chances to learn.

questions.stem_md: Without any formal power over them, Meera, a senior nurse at an imagined clinic in Gwalior, gets the younger nurses to follow new hygiene routines willingly. This shows Meera's

options.text_md: leadership: the ability to influence people to work willingly towards goals

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** leadership: the ability to influence people to work willingly towards goals. Influencing the behaviour of others so that they work willingly towards shared goals is leadership.

questions.stem_md: In the final week before a delivery deadline, the yard manager of Waltair Marine Fittings (imagined) takes every decision himself, gives exact orders and allows no discussion. Which leadership style is this?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Autocratic. A leader who keeps all decision-making power and expects obedience follows the autocratic style.

questions.stem_md: Before changing shift timings at Lakhota Brass Parts (imagined), the plant head calls a meeting, invites suggestions from the workers and then decides along with them. Which leadership style is this?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Democratic (participative). Consulting subordinates and deciding with them is the democratic or participative style.

questions.stem_md: The editor of an imagined travel magazine in Dharamshala gives her experienced writers a broad theme and leaves them free to choose their places, angles and working hours, stepping in only when asked. Which leadership style is this?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Laissez-faire (free-rein). Giving the group almost complete freedom to decide and act is the laissez-faire or free-rein style.

questions.stem_md: At an imagined state transport depot in Jammu, the depot manager decides every leave request strictly according to the rule book and the chain of authority, refusing any exception. Which leadership style is this?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Bureaucratic. Leading by fixed rules, procedures and official channels is the bureaucratic style. (An autocrat decides by personal will, not by the rule book.)

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** A laissez-faire style can work well with highly skilled, self-motivated employees.

**Reason (R):** Under the laissez-faire style, the leader takes all decisions alone.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are false.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** The assertion is true: skilled, self-driven people can use freedom well. The reason is false: under laissez-faire the group decides; deciding alone is autocratic.

questions.stem_md: Under bureaucratic leadership, the leader manages strictly according to rules, procedures and official channels.
questions.solution_md: **True.** True. A bureaucratic leader goes by the book, following set rules, procedures and the chain of authority.

questions.stem_md: Match each leadership style with what the leader of a team of delivery riders would do under it.

match_right.text_md: Assigns routes strictly as laid down in the company manual
Fixes every route himself and expects riders to obey
Lets the riders work out their own routes
Plans the routes after discussing them with the riders

questions.solution_md: **Key:** (a)–(q), (b)–(s), (c)–(r), (d)–(p). Autocratic: leader decides alone. Democratic: decides after consulting. Laissez-faire: group decides. Bureaucratic: rules decide.

questions.stem_md: Identify the leadership style in each situation at Panchganga Leather Works, an imagined footwear unit in Kolhapur: (i) the owner asks the stitchers to vote on the design of a new sandal; (ii) the owner insists that every step in the procedure manual be followed exactly, without exception.
questions.solution_md: Each style identified with a reason from the situation.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) **Democratic (participative):** the owner **involves the stitchers** in the decision through a vote.
(ii) **Bureaucratic:** the owner leads **strictly by rules and procedures** in the manual, allowing no exceptions.

questions.stem_md: What is leadership? Explain the meaning of the democratic and the laissez-faire styles of leadership.
questions.solution_md: Meaning of leadership and of each style.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Leadership** is the ability of a manager to **influence the behaviour of people** so that they work **willingly** towards the group's goals.
2. **Democratic style:** the leader **consults subordinates**, welcomes their ideas and takes decisions **with the group**.
3. **Laissez-faire style:** the leader gives the group **near-complete freedom** to set its own methods and decisions and acts mainly as a **contact and resource person**.

questions.stem_md: Sanjana, sales head of Shevaroy Steel Utensils (imagined), puts her idea of a festive dealer discount into a short voice message in Tamil before sending it to the dealers. Turning the idea into spoken words is called
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** encoding. Converting an idea into words, symbols or gestures that can be sent is encoding; the receiver later decodes it.

questions.stem_md: After a talk on new hygiene steps, the trainer at Rispana Biscuits (imagined) asks each baker to repeat the steps in their own words. The trainer is seeking
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** feedback. The receiver's response, which shows whether the message was understood, is feedback.

questions.stem_md: During a phone call, a dealer of Yamuna Blankets (imagined) cannot hear the new prices clearly because looms are running loudly next to the caller. In the communication process, this disturbance is called
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** noise. Anything that disturbs or distorts a message on its way, such as loud machines, is noise.

questions.stem_md: A notice at Chilika Seafoods (imagined) was translated into Odia using a word for "shift" that can also mean "move house", so workers thought the plant was relocating. Which barrier to communication is this?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Semantic barrier (faulty translation). Barriers arising from words, language and their meanings, including faulty translation, are semantic barriers.

questions.stem_md: Workers at Kundanagari Foundry (imagined) were twice promised higher bonuses that never came. When the manager announced a new bonus scheme, nobody believed him. Which barrier to communication is at work?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Psychological barrier (distrust). Distrust from past experience makes receivers doubt the message; such barriers of attitude and emotion are psychological.

questions.stem_md: At Agnigarh Hospital Supplies (imagined), every suggestion from workers must be written on a set form and signed by three officers before it reaches management, so workers have stopped making suggestions. Which barrier is this?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Organisational barrier (rigid rules and procedures). Barriers created by the firm's rules, structure and procedures are organisational barriers.

questions.stem_md: The production head of Subarnarekha Agro Tools (imagined) never answers workers' questions and looks annoyed whenever they come to him, so they have stopped reporting problems. Which barrier is this?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Personal barrier (attitude of the superior). A superior's unwillingness to listen or to welcome communication from below is a personal barrier.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Using technical jargon with untrained workers can cause a semantic barrier.

**Reason (R):** Feedback is the last element of the communication process.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are false.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Both are true, but the position of feedback in the process does not explain why jargon blocks understanding; that is about words the receiver does not know.

questions.stem_md: Decoding means putting an idea into words, symbols or gestures before sending it.
questions.solution_md: **False.** False. That describes encoding, done by the sender; decoding is the receiver working out the meaning.

questions.stem_md: Complete the analogy. Sender : Encoding :: Receiver : ___
questions.solution_md: The sender encodes the message; the receiver decodes it.

questions.stem_md: State two objectives that the manager of Loktak Fish Farms (imagined), Imphal, can achieve through a weekly meeting with the boat crews.
questions.solution_md: Any two objectives (inform, instruct, motivate, coordinate, educate, get feedback, build relations) linked to the meeting.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **To inform and instruct:** crews learn the week's **catch targets, routes and safety rules**.
2. **To get feedback and build relations:** crews raise **problems and ideas**, which improves trust and **coordination** between boats.

questions.stem_md: Suggest two ways in which the manager of Kundanagari Foundry (imagined) can overcome the distrust that made workers disbelieve the new bonus scheme.
questions.solution_md: Two measures that rebuild trust (consistency, follow-up, two-way talk, written confirmation, listening).

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Act consistently:** pay the bonus **on the promised date** and announce only what will be delivered, so **actions match words**.
2. **Two-way communication:** meet workers, **explain the scheme in writing** and **invite questions**, then follow up on concerns.

questions.stem_md: The manager of an imagined bus depot in Salem announces a new night-route timetable to drivers. Explain the elements of the communication process using this example.
questions.solution_md: All the elements explained in order with the depot example.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Sender and encoding:** the **manager** turns the new timetable into a **clear notice** with times and routes.
2. **Channel, receiver and decoding:** the notice goes on the **board and the drivers' group**; **drivers** read it and work out what it means for their shifts.
3. **Feedback and noise:** drivers **ask questions or confirm**; a **crowded board** or unclear print is noise that can distort the message.

questions.stem_md: At Panchganga Leather Works (imagined), (i) a notice uses the English words "per cent wastage norm" that stitchers do not follow, (ii) workers fear any change means job cuts, and (iii) ideas from the floor must pass through four officers. Identify the barrier in each case and suggest one remedy for each.
questions.solution_md: Each barrier correctly identified with a matching remedy.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) **Semantic barrier:** use **simple Marathi words** and show an example instead of jargon.
(ii) **Psychological barrier (fear):** the owner should **meet workers**, explain the change honestly and **assure** them about jobs.
(iii) **Organisational barrier:** cut the layers; allow a **suggestion box or direct meetings** with the owner.

questions.stem_md:
(a) Define communication. [1]
(b) The new manager of Indravati Forest Produce Cooperative, an imagined society in Jagdalpur, finds that (i) gatherers misread price notices written in formal Hindi, (ii) they distrust the society after earlier delays in payment, and (iii) every complaint must pass through two clerks before he sees it. Identify each barrier and suggest how to overcome it. [3]
(c) Why should the manager seek feedback after making a change? [1]
questions.solution_md: Definition; three barriers identified with remedies; purpose of feedback.

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) **Communication** is the process of **exchanging ideas, facts and feelings** between two or more persons so as to create **common understanding**.

(b) (i) **Semantic barrier:** formal words confuse the gatherers; the manager should use **simple local language, pictures** and read notices aloud at collection points.
(ii) **Psychological barrier (distrust):** past delays make them doubt messages; he should **pay on time**, keep promises and explain any delay openly.
(iii) **Organisational barrier:** too many layers block complaints; he should hold **open meetings** or let gatherers **reach him directly**.

(c) **Feedback** shows whether the gatherers **understood** the change correctly, so he can **correct** any confusion quickly.

questions.stem_md: Read the passage and answer the questions that follow. *(Imagined firm and people, written by SOYL for practice.)*
questions.solution_md:
**(a)** **Correct option: (d)** On-the-job training. Teaching new workers their job at the workplace is on-the-job training.

**(b)** A very wide span; one supervisor cannot give enough attention.

**(c) (i)** Safety need with a matching incentive.

**OR (c) (ii)** Esteem need with a matching incentive.

questions.stem_md: Read the passage and answer the questions that follow. *(Imagined firm and people, written by SOYL for practice.)*
questions.solution_md:
**(a)** **Correct option: (d)** laissez-faire. Leaving skilled carvers free to decide, with help only on request, is the laissez-faire style.

**(b)** She consults the team and decides with them: democratic.

**(c) (i)** Semantic barrier with a remedy.

**OR (c) (ii)** Feedback reveals misunderstanding early so it can be corrected.

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** (d) laissez-faire

**(b)** **Democratic (participative)** style.

children.solution_md: She consults the team and decides with them: democratic.

answer.model_answer_md: **Democratic (participative)** style.
